C1_build.citation: go build / go run / go install are the canonical invocations shown across official Go documentation for building and running packages.
C1_build.justification: go build is the official first-party build command; a module (go.mod) is sufficient with no separate build-config file needed.

C2_test_runner.citation_evidence: <cite index="35-10,35-11">GoTest is built into the Go language itself, so there’s no need to install additional tools. Running go test immediately starts executing your test cases.</cite>
C2_test_runner.justification: go test is a first-party test runner bundled with the toolchain and invoked with a single command.

C3_coverage.citation_evidence: <cite index="1-3">go test -cover # Show coverage go test -coverprofile=c.out # Generate coverage profile go tool cover -html=c.out # View HTML coverage report</cite> and <cite index="9-3">Go has been supporting test code coverage since 1.12 through the -cover option.</cite>
C3_coverage.justification: Coverage is a native flag of go test with no extra tool installation required to obtain a profile.

C4_benchmarking.citation_evidence: <cite index="1-1,1-2">go test -bench=. # Run all benchmarks go test -bench=Add # Run specific benchmark go test -bench=. -benchmem # Include memory stats</cite>
C4_benchmarking.justification: Benchmarking is a native flag/mode of the same go test command, requiring only a Benchmark-prefixed function.

C5_advanced_instrumentation.citation_evidence: <cite index="3-1">To start, run your tests using the race detector (go test -race).</cite> and <cite index="5-1">To build your code with the race detector enabled, just add the -race flag to the command line: $ go test -race mypkg // test the package $ go run -race mysrc.go // compile and run the program $ go build -race mycmd // build the command $ go install -race mypkg // install the package</cite>
C5_advanced_instrumentation.justification: The data race detector is integrated directly into go build/go test/go run/go install via a single -race flag, officially documented and blogged by the Go team.

metric.build_test_integration.notes: Score reflects that Go's build and test workflow (build, unit tests, coverage, benchmarking, race detection) is entirely first-party, toolchain-native, and reachable through a single command family (go build/go test) with no external assembly, per the frozen rubric above.

criteria: C1 (20 pts): An official, first-party build command ships with the toolchain and requires no external build-system configuration for a basic module/package.
C2 (20 pts): An official, first-party test runner/framework ships with the toolchain (not a bolt-on third-party library) and is invoked by a single standard command.
C3 (20 pts): Code coverage measurement is built into the same first-party command (flag-based), producing a profile without extra tooling installation.
C4 (20 pts): Benchmarking is built into the same first-party command (flag-based) rather than requiring a separate benchmarking harness.
C5 (20 pts): At least one advanced correctness/perf instrument (e.g. data-race detector, fuzzing) is integrated directly into the same build/test command surface, usable via a single flag.
rubric.description: Frozen 0-100 proxy rubric for Build/Test Integration, to be applied identically to every language in the fixed 10-language set. Five equally-weighted (20 pts each) criteria assess how tightly the official build and test workflow is integrated into the language's own toolchain versus requiring third-party assembly.
rubric.scale: Sum of the five criteria, each scored 0 or 20 (full credit only if the capability is first-party, toolchain-integrated, and documented as officially supported); 100 = fully integrated first-party build+test+coverage+bench+advanced-instrumentation workflow with no external assembly required.

D1_spec.citation_evidence: <cite index="22-4,22-5,22-6,22-7">This doc explains how to develop a simple set of Go packages inside a module, and it shows how to use the go command to build and test packages. An interactive introduction to Go in four sections. The first section covers basic syntax and data structures; the second discusses methods and interfaces; the third is about Generics; and the fourth introduces Go's concurrency primitives. Each section concludes with a few exercises so you can practice what you've learned.</cite>
D1_spec.justification: go.dev/ref/spec is the official, actively maintained Go language specification, listed among the core official docs on go.dev/doc/.

D2_api_docs.citation_evidence: <cite index="16-4,16-5">Documentation is generated based on Go source code downloaded from the Go Module Mirror at proxy.golang.org/<module>/@v/<version>.zip. New module versions are fetched from index.golang.org and added to pkg.go.dev site every few minutes.</cite>
D2_api_docs.justification: pkg.go.dev auto-generates documentation for the standard library and all published modules directly from source, refreshed automatically and versioned per module release.

D3_tutorials.citation_evidence: <cite index="20-2">It augments the language specification, the Tour of Go, and How to Write Go Code, all of which you should read first.</cite>
D3_tutorials.justification: Official onboarding material includes the interactive Tour of Go, Effective Go, and How to Write Go Code, all first-party and cross-referenced from go.dev/doc/.

D4_doc_comments.citation_evidence: <cite index="14-1,14-2">Godoc is a tool that parses Go source code with comments to generate human-readable documentation in an HTML site. Whatever documentation you see in pkg.go.dev is generated by Godoc.</cite>
D4_doc_comments.justification: Godoc/go doc extract documentation directly from source comments as a first-party toolchain capability, and this is what powers pkg.go.dev.

D5_verified_examples.citation_evidence: <cite index="29-4,29-6">Godoc examples are snippets of Go code that are displayed as package documentation and that are verified by running them as tests. Having executable documentation for a package guarantees that the information will not go out of date as the API changes.</cite>
D5_verified_examples.justification: Go supports testable Example functions that are compiled and executed by go test, comparing captured output against an Output: comment, and the same examples are rendered on pkg.go.dev, guaranteeing they don't drift from the real API.

metric.documentation_quality.notes: Score reflects that Go's documentation stack (spec, pkg.go.dev auto-generated API docs, Tour of Go/Effective Go, godoc comment conventions, and toolchain-verified runnable Example functions) satisfies all five frozen rubric criteria with first-party, toolchain-native mechanisms.

criteria: D1 (20 pts): An official, complete language specification/reference is published and maintained by the language's own project.
D2 (20 pts): Standard-library (and, where applicable, published package) API documentation is auto-generated from source, versioned, and searchable via an official site.
D3 (20 pts): Official first-party tutorials/guides exist for onboarding (e.g., interactive tour, idiomatic-style guide, getting-started doc).
D4 (20 pts): A toolchain-integrated doc-comment convention exists so documentation is extracted automatically from source comments without a third-party generator.
D5 (20 pts): Documentation examples can be executed/verified automatically by the toolchain (not just static prose) to prevent drift from the actual API.
rubric.description: Frozen 0-100 proxy rubric for Documentation Quality, applied identically to every language in the fixed 10-language set. Five equally-weighted (20 pts each) criteria assess availability/completeness of an official language reference, an auto-generated/versioned standard-library API reference, official onboarding tutorials, toolchain-integrated doc-comment conventions, and executable/verifiable documentation examples.
rubric.scale: Sum of the five criteria, each scored 0 or 20; 100 = complete official spec, auto-generated versioned API docs, official tutorials, native doc-comment tooling, and toolchain-verified runnable examples.

sampling_and_methodology.limitation: This packet evaluates only the Go language cell as assigned; the identical rubric text above is frozen for reuse by sibling per-language workers so that all 10 languages in the fixed set are scored against the same criteria, thresholds, and evidence-collection method.
sampling_and_methodology.retrieval_route: web_search tool queries against official go.dev domains and cross-checked secondary sources
sampling_and_methodology.selection_rule: Official first-party language-project documentation (go.dev, pkg.go.dev) preferred as the language-neutral, externally observable authority for this metric; third-party tutorial/blog sources used only to corroborate mechanics (e.g., -race flag behavior, coverage flag behavior) already asserted by the official docs.
